title: Norms
hook: A missing harness becomes a rule only when the whole rescue team has to read the tag.
counterintuition: Norms are not only cooperative tools, but also control tools. A backed rule can stop selfish grabs while deciding which bids for rank must stay hidden.
tryThisNow: Name one rule your group claims to hold. Write the actual sanction beside it: gossip, lost trust, exclusion, formal penalty, or nothing.
keyTakeaway: A norm becomes real when the group can make defiance expensive enough that selfishness has to hide or stop.

breakdown.fastRead:
Mud flakes from the rope bag while Claire counts the harness tags. One strong climber has taken extra gear again. A private scolding would make the problem personal. Claire puts the tags on the table and has every rescuer read the missing numbers aloud.

That is the difference between a preference and a norm. A norm is a rule the group can enforce.

Small groups depend on that force. Gossip, reputation, and shared memory turn selfish grabbing into a public cost. The rule protects cooperation because the violation no longer stays between two people. The room now knows what happened, and the room can remember.
breakdown.deepRead:
Mud flakes from the rope bag onto the gear-room floor when Claire finds the missing harness tags. The strongest climber took two extras again, which means someone else will enter the ravine with less margin. Claire does not start with a speech about fairness. She places the tags on the table and asks each rescuer to read the missing numbers before the team loads the van.

A norm needs backing. Without backing, it is only a wish with better wording. With backing, a selfish move changes price. The person who grabs extra gear now faces reputation, questions, loss of trust, or formal discipline. The group has made the private advantage visible.

In nomadic egalitarian groups of 20-50 members, reputation is not background noise; it is the court. The pattern of gossip and reputation enforcement can punish before any official penalty appears. The idea of weapons as coalition equalizers changes the politics of selfish strength when weaker people can stand together. Once coalitions can check a stronger person, open domination becomes less safe.

The punishment often starts as talk before it becomes anything formal.

This is why norms are both cooperative and controlling. They protect the group from obvious selfish motives, but they also decide which ambitions can be shown. Bragging, currying favor, subgroup politics, and visible grabbing become risky because the group has ways to notice and respond.

The limit is precision. Enforcement can slide into mobbing when suspicion outruns evidence or when the sanction is bigger than the harm. A good norm makes the selfish move costly enough to protect the group, not so vague that anyone can be punished for being disliked.
breakdown.fullRead:
"He only takes Sundays because nobody uses them," Henrik says at the tenant table. Paula opens the complaint log and sees the same name beside the same laundry slot for eight weeks. Everyone has been irritated in private. Nobody has made the pattern common knowledge. So the rule has not been a norm yet. It has been a hope.

Paula writes the laundry rota on the building board, moves the magnetic name strips in public, and asks tenants to initial swaps. The charming rule-bender can still ask for Sunday. He just cannot make the private excuse do all the work. The group has turned quiet resentment into a visible standard.

That is what collective enforcement does. It changes the cost of selfishness. A rule against grabbing, bragging, currying favor, or running subgroup politics only matters if others can notice the violation and respond together. Otherwise the selfish move keeps its reward and pays almost no price.

Picture nomadic egalitarian groups of 20-50 members where nobody can vanish into anonymity. A reputation travels fast because the audience is the whole world that matters. If weapons act as coalition equalizers, weaker members can stand together against a stronger one and selfish strength loses some of its private advantage. The rule gains teeth because the group can back it.

What rule in your life has no teeth at all?

That question is uncomfortable because many groups confuse stated values with norms. A workplace says nobody hoards credit, but the hoarder keeps getting promoted. A club says scarce spots are allocated fairly, but the sponsor's friend always gets the race bib. A team says no bragging around children, but the loud parent controls the sideline mood. In each case, the rule has language. It lacks enforcement.

Graham sees the difference at the rural fire brigade. The thermal camera hook is empty above the training board, and three names have been swapped off the scarce training list after private conversations near the captain's truck. Before fire season, he moves the list to a public board and requires two signatures for every swap. The slots do not become less scarce. The subgroup politics become harder to hide.

Good enforcement is not drama. It is visibility plus proportion. Put the sign-out tags on the table. Post the rota. Require conflicts before grant scoring. Ask the parent to hand the player patch to the defender he ignored. These moves work because they let the group see the rule being backed without turning every breach into a spectacle.

The norm is the backed rule, not the noble phrase. When the backing disappears, visible selfishness returns because it is profitable. When the backing is clear, selfishness must either shrink, disguise itself, or pay the group price.

A norm is strongest when people know how it will be backed before the breach occurs. That backing turns a nice sentence into a shared price for selfishness.

examples.title: Claire Sets Out the Missing Harness Tags

planSpec.audience: a team lead stopping one strong member from taking extra equipment
planSpec.stakes: the norm protects the whole team only if visible grabbing becomes costly
planSpec.requiredBeat: Claire places the sign-out tags on the table and asks every rescuer to read the missing harness numbers aloud before anyone confronts the strongest climber.

examples.scenario: Mud flakes from the rope bag onto the gear-room floor. Claire, the search-and-rescue lead, finds two harness tags missing from the sign-out sheet on Saturday morning. Everyone knows the strongest climber takes extras, but nobody says it near him. Before the team loads the van, Claire places the tags on the table and asks each rescuer to read the missing numbers aloud. She has to decide whether the rule will stay private or become enforceable. The missing tags make the private grab visible before the van leaves, which gives the team a clean enforcement point.
examples.whatToDo: Make the violation visible before making it personal. Put the tags where the whole team can see them, then enforce the gear rule through shared knowledge and a clear sign-out standard.
examples.whyItMatters: The norm protects everyone only when grabbing extra gear carries a group cost. A private scolding leaves the rule dependent on Claire’s nerve.

examples.title: Henrik Defends the Sunday Laundry Grab

planSpec.audience: a tenant board dealing with a charming rule-bender
planSpec.stakes: silent resentment is replacing enforceable standards
planSpec.requiredBeat: "He only takes Sundays because nobody uses them," Henrik says, and Paula turns the private complaints into a posted rotation everyone can verify.

examples.scenario: "He only takes Sundays because nobody uses them," Henrik says at the tenant table. Paula has the laundry rota, magnetic name strips, and complaint log spread across the basement desk. Eight quiet complaints point to the same charming neighbor. Paula has to decide before the meeting ends whether to keep collecting whispers or post a rotation every tenant can verify. The rota board turns private resentment into a standard everyone can inspect before Sunday arrives again.
examples.whatToDo: Post the rotation and require visible swaps. Turn private irritation into a shared record so the rule no longer depends on who is willing to complain in the hallway.
examples.whyItMatters: Silent resentment is weak enforcement. A visible rota makes the standard common knowledge and gives the group a fair way to back it.

examples.title: Nicolas Holds the Sponsor Envelope

planSpec.domain: local running club race bib allocation
planSpec.audience: a club treasurer protecting fair access to a scarce marathon entry
planSpec.stakes: favor-currying could quietly decide who gets the entry
planSpec.requiredBeat: Who gets the bib when the fastest runner also brought the sponsor?

examples.scenario: Who gets the bib when the sponsor is standing beside the fastest runner? Nicolas, the running club treasurer, has one race bib, a sponsor envelope, and the club bylaws on the counter after Tuesday intervals. The fastest runner smiles and says the sponsor prefers a strong showing. Nicolas must decide whether the bib goes by the posted rule or by a favor that everyone can pretend is merit. The bib checkout list gives the sponsor less room to treat a friendship as an exception nobody else can see.
examples.whatToDo: Read the allocation rule aloud and record the decision beside the bylaws. If the sponsor has a case, make it public before the bib moves hands.
examples.whyItMatters: Scarce spots create pressure for favor-currying. The norm survives only if the group can see why the exception was allowed or refused.

examples.title: Graham Moves the Training List Into View

planSpec.audience: a captain preventing status from capturing scarce training
planSpec.stakes: bragging and subgroup politics can split the brigade before fire season
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sam moves the training list from the captain's truck window to a public board and requires two signatures for every swap.

examples.scenario: The empty hook for the thermal camera sits above the training board. Graham, the brigade captain, used to leave the scarce training list taped inside his truck window, where swaps happened after private jokes and subgroup pressure. Before fire season, he moves the list to the public board and requires two signatures for every swap. Bragging still happens, but it no longer quietly captures the slots. The patch has to move through the child’s hands, so the apology becomes part of the group rule rather than a speech by adults.
examples.whatToDo: Move scarce allocation into public view and require visible swap records. Make the norm boring, checkable, and harder to bend through private status games.
examples.whyItMatters: Training slots carry prestige. A public board turns reputation pressure toward fairness instead of letting subgroup politics decide from the truck window.

examples.title: Aanya Reopens the Friendly Emails

planSpec.audience: a chair stopping reputation deals from shaping grant rankings
planSpec.stakes: review norms fail if whispered bargains stay below common knowledge
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Aanya one leaked ranking to see that private praise had become currency, so she makes conflicts and prior favors visible before scoring begins.

examples.scenario: It took Aanya one leaked ranking at the city grant office to reread every friendly email. The rubric looked clean, but the review packets had moved after private praise between committee members. As chair, she must decide whether to treat the leak as gossip or require conflict notes before the next scoring session. The leaked ranking shows why private praise must be logged before the next packet is scored.
examples.whatToDo: Move prior favors into the formal record before scores are assigned. Make reviewers name debts and conflicts while the rubric is still open.
examples.whyItMatters: Review norms fail when private praise becomes currency. Common knowledge gives the committee a way to enforce fairness before rankings harden.

examples.title: Nicolas Hands the Patch Away

planSpec.audience: a coach enforcing anti-bragging norms around ten-year-olds
planSpec.stakes: a parent's visible self-promotion is teaching the team what the group tolerates
planSpec.requiredBeat: You ask Nicolas to hand the player-of-the-week patch to the quiet defender he ignored, making the group reward the norm instead of the boast.

examples.scenario: You hear the parent narrating his child’s goal before the kids reach halftime. Coach Paula stands inside the sideline rope with the player patch in her hand and the orange cones stacked behind her. Nicolas, the loud parent, keeps praising only his scorer. Paula asks him to hand the patch to the quiet defender he ignored, making the group reward the norm instead of the boast. The camera hook is empty now, which makes the cost of private list-swapping visible before fire season.
examples.whatToDo: Redirect the public reward toward the ignored contribution. Let Nicolas participate in honoring the norm so the group sees what behavior earns attention.
examples.whyItMatters: A bragging parent teaches children what the group tolerates. Publicly rewarding the quieter contribution makes the anti-bragging norm visible without a lecture.

questions.prompt: A club says members take turns with a scarce resource, but nobody tracks swaps or reacts when one person takes extra. What is missing? In the storage room, the sign-up sheet is blank and the spare key hangs beside the door.
choices: A clearer slogan about fairness.
A sanction or shared record that makes defiance costly.
A more generous attitude toward strong members.
questions.explanation: A norm needs backing. The shared record or sanction changes the cost of defiance, while a slogan leaves the rule at the level of preference.

questions.prompt: A volunteer team knows one person hoards equipment. Which first move best creates enforceable pressure without turning it into a duel? The cases are stacked behind the stage, and the setup crew has fifteen minutes before guests arrive.
choices: Put the sign-out record in front of the team before confronting anyone.
Ask the hoarder privately to be more considerate.
Let the strongest member take extra gear because skill earns privilege.
questions.explanation: The public record turns private suspicion into common knowledge. A private request may help once, and skill privilege destroys the cooperative rule.

questions.prompt: A tenant board has many hallway complaints about the same laundry-slot grab, but no posted rotation. Which action best turns irritation into a norm? The basement calendar is smudged, and residents keep finding wet clothes piled on the folding table.
choices: Tell tenants to stop gossiping.
Post a rota with visible swap initials.
Let the charming tenant keep Sundays to avoid conflict.
questions.explanation: The rota gives everyone the same evidence and a way to enforce the rule. Ending gossip removes one pressure channel, and avoiding conflict rewards the violation.

questions.prompt: At a grant committee table, reviewers ban conflicts but let old favors stay private while one scarce award is scored. What weak point keeps the norm from being enforceable? Two finalists have equal files, and the chair keeps glancing at a colleague who helped him last year.
choices: The grant rubric has too many categories.
The committee should trust expert judgment without forms.
The conflict norm lacks common knowledge before scoring.
questions.explanation: Private favors can steer rankings if nobody has to name them. The rubric may be fine; the enforcement problem is that hidden debts never become visible.

questions.prompt: A coach wants to stop sideline bragging around ten-year-olds. Which move best backs the norm? The parents are lined along the fence, and the loudest child keeps turning every drill into a status show.
choices: Ask the loud parent to publicly recognize the overlooked defender.
Tell every parent that bragging is unattractive.
Cancel the weekly patch so nobody can compete for praise.
questions.explanation: The public patch shifts reward toward the desired standard. A lecture is weak backing, and canceling all praise removes a useful tool for enforcement.

questions.prompt: A fire brigade keeps training slots on a private truck-window list, and swaps follow status pressure. What should the captain change? The younger members see the chalk marks only after the senior crew has already claimed the best times.
choices: Choose the strongest members and stop pretending slots are fair.
Move the list to a public board and require signed swaps.
Delay all training until nobody wants the slots.
questions.explanation: The public list and signatures make subgroup pressure harder to hide. Choosing only strength abandons the norm, and delay dodges the allocation problem.

questions.prompt: A group punishes a vague rumor before anyone can inspect evidence. What is the strongest objection from a norm-enforcement view? The accusation moves through the chat before the accused member can show receipts or name witnesses.
choices: The sanction is not backed by enough shared evidence.
The group should never enforce norms through reputation.
The accused person must be innocent if the rule is vague.
questions.explanation: Enforcement needs visibility and proportion. Reputation can enforce norms, but punishment outrunning evidence becomes mobbing rather than rule backing.

questions.prompt: A workplace praises fairness but keeps promoting the person who visibly grabs credit. What does that reveal about the fairness rule? The quarterly meeting applauds teamwork while the same employee presents everyone else’s work as his own.
choices: It is probably a backed norm because people mention it often.
It is only about private feelings, not public behavior.
It lacks a real group cost for defiance.
questions.explanation: Promotion rewards the violation, so the rule lacks teeth. Frequent praise of fairness does not create a norm if selfish credit-taking keeps paying.

questions.prompt: In a professional association, one scarce conference seat keeps going to people who praised the chair in private emails. Which design makes the norm against favor-currying easier to enforce? The nomination inbox is private, and the small panel has to publish a decision by Friday.
choices: A written exception rule read before the seat is assigned.
A private promise that members will be objective.
A chair who decides alone to avoid gossip.
questions.explanation: A written exception rule creates common evidence before the decision. Private promises are weak, and solo decisions remove the group’s enforcement role.

reviewCards.front: A group says it has a rule, but violations keep paying. What should you inspect?
reviewCards.back: Inspect the backing. A norm is real only when the group can impose a cost through reputation, lost trust, exclusion, formal penalty, or another shared sanction.

reviewCards.front: Why does common knowledge matter when someone bends a rule in public?
reviewCards.back: Common knowledge lets the group act together. Private suspicion leaves each person isolated, while shared evidence makes enforcement less risky and less personal.

reviewCards.front: A strong member keeps taking more than their share. What turns the rule into enforcement?
reviewCards.back: Make the taking visible to the group and tie it to a clear sanction or record. The rule starts working when the advantage carries a cost.

reviewCards.front: When can norm enforcement become dangerous?
reviewCards.back: When the group punishes without enough evidence, uses a vague standard, or makes the sanction larger than the violation. Good enforcement is visible and proportionate.

reviewCards.front: What do gossip and reputation do in a norm system?
reviewCards.back: They carry enforcement before formal penalties appear. Talk and memory can make visible selfishness costly enough that people hide it, stop it, or pay for it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Read norms as backed rules. When a group claims to value something, look for the record, witness, sanction, or reputation cost that makes defiance expensive.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a rule keeps being violated, then ask what evidence would make the violation visible to everyone affected.
If private complaints are piling up, then turn the pattern into a shared log before naming blame.
If one person uses charm or rank to bend a scarce-resource rule, then make exceptions public before granting one.
If you rely on a norm, then write what cost you are willing to support when someone breaks it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one rule your group talks about. Write the rule, the current sanction, and one evidence source that would make enforcement fairer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, watch one repeated irritation in a group. Do not start with blame. Map the rule, the violation, who knows, and what cost would make the rule real.

memorableLines.text: A norm is a rule the group can enforce.
memorableLines.why: It strips the concept down to the one feature that matters for action.

memorableLines.text: The punishment often starts as talk before it becomes anything formal.
memorableLines.why: It makes gossip and reputation visible as enforcement tools instead of side noise.

memorableLines.text: The norm is the backed rule, not the noble phrase.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a compact test for separating stated values from enforceable standards.
